problem: Prior active visual search (AVS) methods either need large offline RL training that may not transfer to the deployed environment, or (POMP, POMCP-based) require a known 2D floor map. Standard POMCP cannot handle a state space that grows as the map is built online.
motivation: Robots deployed in unknown indoor environments need a training-free online planner that does not depend on pre-collected data or a known floor map. Standard POMCP belief reinvigoration assumes a fixed state set and penalises newly added states, discouraging exploration of newly discovered frontiers.
key_idea: Formulate AVS in unknown environments as a POMDP whose states (pose graph plus frontier candidate cells) grow online, and solve it with POMCP using a two-step belief reinvigoration that preserves old particles and adds uniform particles over new candidate cells.
insight: The ablation shows that the new belief reinvigoration is the main source of gain: POMCP with known map (POMP) at SR 0.56 on AVD Hard rises to 0.86 with the new reinvigoration (POMP+), and POMP++ without a known map reaches 0.84. The gain comes at the cost of longer paths (APL 33.71 vs 20.05). Detector quality matters greatly: with a real detector SR roughly halves (0.84 to 0.41).
method: Environment map: grid with four cell types (occluder, seen, candidate/frontier, unknown), updated each step from RGB-D scene reconstruction (Alg. 1)
Pose graph: nodes are reachable robot poses in seen cells, edges are single-action transitions; grows as exploration proceeds

Dynamic POMDP: states = target in a specific candidate cell combined with robot pose; transition model from graph edges; observation model from a pose-to-candidate visibility function; reward +1000 on detection and -1 per step
POMCP planner: beta simulations per step over the current state set, with the map fixed during simulation; the action with highest value is executed

Two-step belief reinvigoration: (1) keep all particles of B_t and remove only those whose simulated observation differs from the real one; (2) add new particles sampled uniformly over newly discovered candidate cells, with a tunable percentage
Robust visual docking: once the target is detected, approach it via the shortest path on the pose graph with re-planning (as in POMP)

setting.backbone: POMCP online planner (no learned policy); Mask-RCNN ResNet50 (MS-COCO pretrained) detector on Habitat, GT annotations or AVD detector on AVD
setting.training_data: none (training-free planner; detector pretrained on MS-COCO for Habitat)
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: Forward/Backward/Turn_Left/Turn_Right/Stop (AVD: 30 cm, 30°); Habitat: Forward 25 cm, Turn 30°, Stop
setting.simulator: Active Vision Dataset (real captured grid) and Habitat (Matterport3D)
setting.privileged: GT object annotations for detection on AVD main results; GT semantic segmentation used to reconstruct walls online in Habitat

numbers.eval_set_note: 3 test scenes (Home_005_1 easy, Home_001_2 medium, Home_003_2 hard), subset of objects, EAT/POMP protocol, 125 step limit
numbers.extra: no known floor map; GT detection; average over the three scenes
numbers.evidence: Table I, Avg. columns, POMP++ row

numbers.eval_set_note: 11 Matterport3D validation scenes (paper describes as Habitat ObjectNav Challenge; MP3D scenes actually)
numbers.extra: 6 target categories (chair, couch, potted plant, bed, toilet, tv); walls from GT semantic segmentation
numbers.evidence: Table II: POMP++ SPL 0.148, SR 0.420, DTS 3.726

numbers_note: The Habitat benchmark is on Matterport3D scenes (bench label may better be MP3D-ObjNav). AVD numbers are in Table I. Metrics printed as fractions (0-1).
results: On AVD, POMP++ achieves avg SR 0.87 vs EAT 0.69 and POMP (known map) 0.76, with longer paths. On Habitat ObjectNav (MP3D val), SR 0.420 vs SemExp 0.360, SPL 0.148 vs 0.144, and DTS 3.726 vs 6.733.
limitations: Lower path efficiency (APL/ASPPL) than baselines since it explores more
Performance drops sharply with a real object detector (SR roughly halves)
Uses GT semantic segmentation for walls and GT detections in main experiments; only 2D geometric reasoning, no semantic priors
